lessons.title: Young's Double Slit Experiment
lessons.content:
In 1801 Thomas Young passed light from a single narrow slit through two very close parallel slits and onto a screen. The two slits act as two coherent sources: they send out light of the same frequency that stays in step, because both are lit by the same source. Where the light from the two slits arrives in step, the waves reinforce each other and a bright fringe appears; where it arrives out of step, the waves cancel each other and a dark fringe appears. The result is a pattern of equally spaced bright and dark bands called interference fringes.

The experiment is direct evidence that light is a wave, and the pattern can be used to measure the wavelength of the light. The fringe spacing x = wavelength x D / a, where D is the distance from the slits to the screen and a is the separation of the two slits. Increasing the distance to the screen widens the fringes, moving the slits closer together widens them, and using red light instead of blue light widens them as well, because red light has the longer wavelength.

In the laboratory a laser or a lamp behind a single slit provides the coherent light, and the fringes are viewed on a screen or through a travelling microscope so that the distance across several fringes can be measured and divided to give the spacing of one. A stream of particles passing through two slits would simply give two bright bands, so the alternating bright and dark fringes cannot be explained by the corpuscular theory.

Interference fringes: the equally spaced bright and dark bands produced where light from the two slits overlaps.
Fringe spacing: x = wavelength x D / a, where D is the distance from the slits to the screen and a is the slit separation.

lessons.title: Rectilinear Propagation of Light
lessons.content:
Light travels in straight lines through a uniform medium. This is called rectilinear propagation, and it is the reason we draw rays, which are straight lines with arrowheads showing the direction of travel, and beams, which are bundles of rays. The straight-line model is an approximation, because light spreads a little when it passes a narrow gap, but it explains almost every everyday observation of light.

A shadow forms because light travels in straight lines and cannot bend around an object: the shadow is the region behind the object that the light cannot reach. A point source gives a sharp shadow with one fully dark region, called the umbra. An extended source such as a fluorescent tube gives a dark umbra with a partly lit region around it, called the penumbra, because light from different parts of the source is blocked by different amounts. A solar eclipse happens when the Moon's shadow falls on the Earth, and a lunar eclipse when the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon; in each case the sharp edge of the shadow is itself evidence that light travels in straight lines.

A pin-hole camera uses rectilinear propagation to form a real, inverted image. Light from the top of the object passes through the hole and lands near the bottom of the screen, and light from the bottom lands near the top, so the image is upside down and laterally inverted. The image is sharpest when the hole is small, and its magnification is the image distance divided by the object distance. Making the hole larger lets in more light but blurs the image, because every point of the object then sends a cone of light through the hole instead of a single ray.

Umbra and penumbra: the fully dark part of a shadow and the partly lit region around it cast by an extended source.
Pin-hole camera: a small hole forms a real, inverted image because light travels in straight lines.

lessons.title: Focal Length Determination
lessons.content:
The focal length of a converging lens is the distance from the optical centre to the principal focus, the point where rays parallel to the principal axis meet after passing through the lens. In the distant object method an object as far away as possible, such as a window or a distant tree, is used so that the rays arriving at the lens are nearly parallel; the image then forms at the principal focus, and the distance from the lens to a screen showing the sharpest image is the focal length. The method is quick, but it works only if the object really is far enough away.

The u-v method is more accurate. A converging lens is set up on an optical bench with an object such as an illuminated cross-wire at one end and a screen at the other. For each position of the object the screen is moved until a sharp image is formed, and the object distance u and the image distance v are measured from the optical centre and put into the lens formula 1 / f = 1 / u + 1 / v. Several pairs of readings are taken and the average focal length is found, or the results are plotted as a graph of 1 / v against 1 / u, which is a straight line; the intercepts of that line give 1 / f, so the reciprocal of the intercept is the focal length. Averaging several readings reduces the effect of an error in any one of them.

Inaccurate results come from measuring u and v from the wrong point instead of from the optical centre, from judging the sharpest image by eye, and from the screen not being square to the principal axis. In the plane mirror method the lens rests on a plane mirror with a pin held above it; the pin is moved until it coincides exactly with its own image, and at that position the pin is at the principal focus, so the distance from the pin to the lens is the focal length. Whichever method is used, the answer is checked against the value marked on the lens.

u-v method: the object and image distances are measured and put into the lens formula 1 / f = 1 / u + 1 / v.
Graph method: a graph of 1 / v against 1 / u is a straight line whose intercepts give 1 / f.

lessons.title: Current, Voltage, and Resistance
lessons.content:
Electricity is the flow of electric charge, usually carried by electrons through a conductor. Current (I) is the rate of flow of charge, measured in Amperes (A). Voltage (V), or potential difference, is the energy per unit charge that 'pushes' the current through the circuit, measured in Volts (V). Resistance (R) is the opposition to the flow of current, measured in Ohms (Ω).

The relationship between these three quantities is known as Ohm's Law: V = IR. This law states that for many materials, the current is directly proportional to the voltage applied, provided the temperature remains constant. Components like resistors follow this law, while others like light bulbs change their resistance as they get hotter.

In CSEC Physics, you will build and analyse series and parallel circuits. In a series circuit, there is only one path for the current, so it remains the same everywhere. In a parallel circuit, there are multiple paths, and the total current is the sum of the currents in each branch. You will also learn to calculate total resistance for both types of arrangements and use multimeters to take measurements.

The key that comes with the diagrams names the circuit symbols used: the battery (the long plate is the positive terminal), the resistor and the bulb. In the parallel arrangement each branch is connected across the same potential difference, so the same 6 V battery drives 3 A through a 2 Ω branch and 2 A through a 3 Ω branch, a total of 5 A; in series it drives one current of 1 A through a 2 Ω and a 4 Ω resistor, leaving 2 V across the 2 Ω resistor and 4 V across the 4 Ω resistor.

Materials differ in how easily charge moves through them. A conductor lets charge flow easily: in a metal such as copper or aluminium each atom gives up one or more electrons that are free to move through the metal, so the current is a flow of free electrons. An electrolyte such as dilute sulphuric acid or salt solution also conducts, but there the current is carried by ions, the charged particles into which the substance splits, and the positive and negative ions move in opposite directions through the solution.

An insulator holds its electrons tightly, so charge cannot flow through it: plastic, rubber, glass, dry wood and dry air are insulators, which is why a wire is covered with plastic and the body of a switch is made of plastic or ceramic. In a metal the current is a flow of electrons from the negative terminal towards the positive terminal and in an electrolyte it is a flow of ions, but in both cases the conventional current in the circuit is taken to flow from the positive terminal to the negative terminal.

Resistance (R) opposes the flow of current.
Conductor: a material in which charge flows easily, such as a metal or an electrolyte.
Insulator: a material that does not let charge flow, such as plastic, rubber or dry air.
Metals conduct by the movement of free electrons, while electrolytes conduct by the movement of ions.

lessons.title: Magnetism and Electromagnetism
lessons.content:
A magnet has a north and a south pole, and like poles repel while unlike poles attract. Magnetic materials such as iron, steel, cobalt and nickel are attracted to a magnet. The pattern of a magnetic field can be shown with iron filings or plotting compasses, and the field lines run from north to south outside the magnet.

When current flows through a wire a magnetic field is produced around it, and the field is stronger if the current is larger or the wire is wound into a coil. Winding the wire around a soft iron core produces an electromagnet, which is magnetised while the current flows and demagnetised when it stops — the basis of relays, electric bells and lifting magnets. Reversing the current reverses the poles, and the direction is given by the right-hand grip rule.

Electromagnetic induction works the other way round: moving a magnet into or out of a coil, or moving a coil in a magnetic field, generates a voltage across the coil. A faster movement or a stronger field gives a bigger voltage. This is how generators and dynamos produce electricity. A transformer uses two coils wound on the same iron core to change an alternating voltage: the ratio of the voltages equals the ratio of the numbers of turns, and a step-up transformer has more turns on the output coil.

Magnetic flux density is the quantity that describes how strong a magnetic field is: it is the magnetic flux passing through unit area at right angles to the field, B = flux / area, and its direction is the direction of the field line at that point. Magnetic flux is measured in webers (Wb), and the SI unit of magnetic flux density is the tesla (T), where 1 T = 1 Wb/m2. The Earth's magnetic field at the surface is only about 0.05 mT, while the field of a strong electromagnet or an MRI scanner reaches 1 T or more. Read the unit in the question before you answer: the tesla measures magnetic flux density B, the weber measures magnetic flux, and the henry measures inductance.

A changing magnetic field through a conductor induces a voltage, and the voltage produced in this way is called an induced electromotive force. The size of the induced electromotive force depends on how fast the field through the coil changes and on the number of turns on the coil: pulling a magnet slowly out of a coil gives a small reading, plunging it in quickly gives a large one, and a coil of many turns gives a bigger voltage than a coil of few turns because each turn adds to the total. This is Faraday's law: the induced electromotive force is proportional to the rate of change of the magnetic field through the coil.

The direction of the induced current is given by Lenz's law: the induced current always flows in the direction that opposes the change producing it. Pushing a magnet into a coil induces a current that tries to push it back out, and pulling the magnet out induces a current that tries to hold it in. The rule is the conservation of energy at work in induction, because the induced current has to be paid for by the work done against that opposing force, and it is the reason a generator becomes harder to turn as the current it supplies increases.

An a.c. generator, or alternator, is a coil turning in a magnetic field. The ends of the coil are joined to two slip rings, and carbon brushes press on the slip rings so that the current reaches the external circuit while the coil rotates freely. Because each side of the coil moves across the field first one way and then the other, the current reverses direction every half turn, and the output is an alternating voltage that follows a sine curve. The frequency of the supply equals the number of revolutions per second of the coil, which is 50 hertz for the mains in the Caribbean, and the peak value is the largest voltage or current the output reaches, which grows if the magnetic field is stronger or the coil has more turns. A d.c. dynamo is built with a split-ring commutator instead of slip rings, so the current in the external circuit is always in the same direction even though the current inside the rotating coil still reverses each half turn.

A transformer changes the size of an alternating voltage: the ratio of the primary voltage to the secondary voltage equals the ratio of the number of turns on the two coils, so a step-up transformer has more turns on the secondary coil and gives a larger output voltage, while a step-down transformer has fewer and gives a smaller one. A transformer works only with an alternating supply, because a direct voltage sets up a field in the core that does not change and so induces nothing in the secondary coil. In an ideal transformer the power input equals the power output, so when the voltage is stepped up the current is stepped down by the same factor, and the efficiency of a transformer is the useful power output divided by the power input, written as a percentage. A real transformer loses a little energy, and a laminated core reduces the losses from eddy currents while thick copper coils keep the resistance low, so a large transformer can be over 95 per cent efficient. Electricity is transmitted at a high voltage so that the current in the cables is small, because the energy wasted as heat in a cable depends on the square of the current; a step-down transformer near the user then brings the voltage down to a safe level.

Electromagnetic induction: generating a voltage by moving a magnet and a coil relative to each other.
Transformer: two coils on one iron core that change an alternating voltage; the voltage ratio equals the turns ratio.
Magnetic flux density: the magnetic flux passing through unit area at right angles to the field, measured in tesla (T).

Induced electromotive force: the voltage induced across a conductor when the magnetic field through it changes; it grows with the rate of change of the field and with the number of turns on the coil (Faraday's law).
Lenz's law: the induced current flows in the direction that opposes the change producing it.
A.c. generator: a coil turning in a magnetic field, with slip rings carrying an alternating output whose frequency equals the number of revolutions per second of the coil.
Peak value: the largest voltage or current an alternating supply reaches in each cycle, which grows with a stronger field or more turns on the coil.
Transformer efficiency: in an ideal transformer the power input equals the power output, and efficiency = useful power output / power input x 100%.

lessons.title: Electrical Power and Safety
lessons.content:
Electrical power is the rate at which electrical energy is transferred: power = voltage x current, P = VI, measured in watts. Combining this with resistance gives P = I squared R. The energy transferred by an appliance is found from energy = power x time, and domestic electrical energy is sold in kilowatt-hours (kWh), where 1 kWh is the energy a 1 kW appliance transfers in 1 hour.

Domestic circuits are wired in parallel so each appliance gets the full mains voltage and can be switched independently. The three-pin plug has a live wire (brown), a neutral wire (blue) and an earth wire (green and yellow). Appliances with metal cases are earthed so that if the live wire touches the case the current flows safely to earth instead of through the user.

A fuse is a thin wire that melts and breaks the circuit if the current exceeds its rating, and a circuit breaker does the same job with a switch that can be reset. Choosing the correct fuse rating matters: too small and it blows in normal use, too large and it fails to protect. The live wire is connected through the fuse or breaker so that the appliance is isolated from the live supply when it operates.

The heating effect of current is the transfer of electrical energy into thermal energy when a current flows through a resistance, and P = I squared R gives the rate at which that energy appears as heat. Appliances that are meant to get hot use this effect in their heating element: an electric kettle, an iron, a toaster and a room heater all pass a current through a resistance to produce heat, and in a filament lamp the wire is heated until it glows. In other appliances the same heating effect is wasted: the warmth of a motor, a battery charger or a transformer is energy that has not done the useful job, and a fuse is simply a thin wire chosen so that the heating effect melts it when the current becomes dangerously large.

Describe the live, neutral and earth wires and why appliances are earthed
Explain the action of fuses and circuit breakers

Kilowatt-hour: the energy a 1 kW appliance transfers in one hour; the unit domestic electricity is sold in.
Earthing: connecting a metal case to earth so a fault current flows to earth instead of through a person.
Heating effect of current: the transfer of electrical energy into thermal energy when a current flows through a resistance, at a rate given by P = I squared R.

lessons.title: Charging by Friction and Induction
lessons.content:
All matter is made of atoms containing protons, neutrons and electrons. Protons carry positive charge, electrons carry an equal negative charge and neutrons carry none. A body is normally neutral because it contains equal numbers of protons and electrons, and the only charged particle that moves from one body to another in everyday charging is the electron. A body that gains electrons becomes negatively charged, and a body that loses electrons is left positively charged.

Charging by friction happens when two different insulators are rubbed together. Rubbing a polythene rod with a dry cloth transfers electrons from the cloth to the rod, so the polythene rod becomes negatively charged while the cloth is left with an equal positive charge. Rubbing a perspex rod transfers electrons in the opposite direction, so the perspex rod becomes positively charged. The two bodies end with equal and opposite charges, because charge is conserved and no charge is created or destroyed.

Charging by induction charges a conductor without touching it with the charged body. When a charged rod is brought near a neutral conductor, the charges inside the conductor separate: charges of the same sign as the rod are repelled towards the far end and charges of the opposite sign are attracted towards the near end. The conductor is earthed while the charged rod is near it, so the repelled charge escapes to earth; the earth connection is then removed and the rod taken away, leaving the conductor charged with the opposite sign to the rod. Nothing is transferred from the rod itself: the conductor is charged by separation and earthing.

Charging by induction: bringing a charged body near a conductor, earthing it, and removing the earth to leave it charged.
Conservation of charge: charge is never created or destroyed, only transferred from one body to another.

lessons.title: Forces Between Charges
lessons.content:
An electric charge exerts a force on any other charge near it. Two like charges repel each other, so the force pushes them apart. Two unlike charges attract each other, so the force pulls them together. The force acts along the line joining the two charges, and it is strongest when the charges are close together.

The size of the force depends on the size of the charges and on the distance between them. Doubling the size of one charge doubles the force between the charges. Doubling the distance between the charges reduces the force to one quarter of its former value, because the force obeys an inverse square law: the force is proportional to the product of the two charges divided by the square of their separation, so force is proportional to (Q1 x Q2) / r squared.

Forces between charges always come in pairs. The force on each charge is equal in size and opposite in direction to the force on the other, so the two charges are pushed apart or pulled together along the same line. This is Newton's third law acting on electric charges.

The force is proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.

lessons.title: Electric Fields
lessons.content:
An electric field is a region in which a charge experiences a force. The direction of the field at a point is the direction of the force on a small positive test charge placed there, so the field points away from a positive charge and towards a negative charge.

Field lines are drawn with arrows to show the direction of the field. Around a single point charge the field is a radial field, and the lines spread out as they get further from the charge. Further apart field lines mean a weaker field. Field lines never cross, because a charge placed at one point cannot be pushed in two directions at once.

Between two parallel plates connected to a supply the field is a uniform field. The field lines are parallel and equally spaced, and a small charge feels the same force everywhere between the plates. Electric field strength is the force per unit charge, E = F / Q, measured in newtons per coulomb.

concepts: Electric field: a region where a charge experiences a force; the field direction is the force direction on a positive test charge.
Radial field: the field around a point charge, with field lines spreading out and weakening with distance.
Uniform field: the parallel, equally spaced field between two parallel plates, where the force on a charge does not change.

lessons.title: Static Charge Applications and Hazards
lessons.content:
Useful applications of static charge are found in industry and in the home. In an electrostatic paint sprayer the paint droplets are given a charge and are attracted to the earthed metal object being painted, so less paint is wasted and the coat is even. A photocopier attracts toner powder to a charged drum, and an electrostatic precipitator in a power station chimney charges the dust particles and collects them on charged plates, which removes dust from the gas leaving the chimney.

Hazards from static charge appear wherever a spark could ignite a fuel or damage a component. Friction between a road tanker and the air, or between fuel and a pipe, builds up charge, and a spark from that charge could ignite petrol vapour, so tankers are earthed and the pipe is bonded to the tanker before fuel is transferred. The same danger exists when refuelling an aircraft, when using flammable solvents, and in a flour mill, where charged dust particles can cause a dust explosion.

Static charge also damages electronic components, especially the metal-oxide parts inside a computer, so engineers wear an earthed wrist strap and work on an earthed mat. Lightning is the largest natural example of static charge: charge builds up in a cloud until the air breaks down and a huge spark carries the charge to earth.

Charged droplets, toner and dust can be steered by an electric field, which is the basis of spray painting, photocopying and dust extraction.
A spark from built-up static charge can ignite flammable vapour or dust, and a sudden discharge can destroy sensitive electronic components.

lessons.title: Direct and Alternating Current
lessons.content:
A direct current, or d.c., flows in one direction only. A cell, a battery or a solar cell supplies direct current, and the output of a d.c. generator is direct current too, so the current keeps the same steady direction as long as the circuit is complete. A d.c. supply has fixed positive and negative terminals, so the current always leaves the same terminal.

An alternating current, or a.c., reverses direction at a regular frequency, so the current flows one way and then the other. An alternating current is supplied by an a.c. generator, and the frequency of the supply is the number of complete cycles each second. The mains supply in the Caribbean is an alternating supply at a frequency of 50 hertz, so the current completes 50 cycles every second and changes direction 100 times.

The two kinds of supply look different on a graph of current against time. A steady direct current is a straight horizontal line on the graph, while an alternating current reaches a peak one way and then a peak the other way, passing through zero in between. The mains is alternating rather than direct for a practical reason: a transformer can change only an alternating voltage. The two wires of an a.c. supply swap their polarity every half cycle, while the terminals of a battery never do.

Alternating current: a current that reverses direction at a regular frequency, supplied by an a.c. generator and used for the mains.
Frequency of the mains: the number of complete cycles each second, which is 50 hertz in the Caribbean.

lessons.title: Primary and Secondary Cells
lessons.content:
A cell changes chemical energy into electrical energy. The electromotive force of a cell, usually shortened to e.m.f., is the energy the cell gives to each unit of charge that passes through it, measured in volts. Every cell has its own resistance, called internal resistance, so while a current flows the voltage measured across the terminals of the cell is a little less than its electromotive force: the difference is the voltage lost inside the cell, and it grows as the current grows.

Cells come in two kinds. A primary cell cannot be recharged, because its chemical reaction cannot be reversed: in a dry cell its chemicals are used up as it delivers charge, so a flat dry cell is thrown away and replaced. A secondary cell, also called an accumulator, can be recharged, because passing a current through it in the opposite direction reverses the chemical reaction and restores the chemicals. The lead-acid accumulator in a car is a secondary cell: each cell gives about 2 volts, and six of them joined in series give the 12 volts of a car battery. The lithium-ion cell in a phone or a laptop is a secondary cell too, and it stores more energy for its mass than a lead-acid cell.

The choice between the two depends on the job. A primary cell is cheap and ready to use with no charging, which suits a torch, a clock or a smoke alarm, but a flat one must be replaced and its chemicals disposed of carefully rather than put in the household rubbish. A secondary cell costs more at the start and has to be charged, but it can be used again hundreds of times, which suits a car, a phone, a power tool or a laptop. The capacity of a cell is the charge it can deliver, measured in ampere-hours: a cell rated at 2 ampere-hours can deliver 2 amperes for one hour, or 1 ampere for two hours.

Explain the electromotive force and the internal resistance of a cell
Give an example of each kind of cell and say what each is used for
concepts: Electromotive force (e.m.f.): the energy a cell gives to each unit of charge, measured in volts.
Internal resistance: the resistance inside a cell, which makes the terminal voltage less than the electromotive force while a current flows.
Primary cell: a cell whose reaction cannot be reversed, such as a dry cell; secondary cell: a cell that can be recharged, such as the lead-acid accumulator or a lithium-ion cell.

lessons.title: Semiconductor Diodes and Rectification
lessons.content:
A semiconductor such as silicon conducts only weakly when it is pure, but its conductivity can be increased by adding a small amount of another element. Joining a p-type region to an n-type region makes a p-n junction, which is the heart of a diode. A diode is a semiconductor component that lets current flow in one direction only, so it acts as a one-way valve in a circuit.

In forward bias the anode is made positive with respect to the cathode, and the diode conducts, so current flows easily. In reverse bias the anode is made negative with respect to the cathode, and the diode blocks the current. A light-emitting diode, or LED, is a diode that gives out light when it conducts in the forward direction, which is why LEDs are used for indicator lamps, torches and television screens.

Because it conducts in one direction only, a diode can change alternating current into direct current, and this process is called rectification. In half-wave rectification one diode lets only half of the cycle reach the output, because the other half reverse biases it. In full-wave rectification four diodes in a bridge turn both halves of the cycle into direct current, and a smoothing capacitor stores charge and keeps the output voltage steady between the pulses. Rectification is used in the power supply of every phone charger and radio.

Explain half-wave and full-wave rectification
Explain the part played by a smoothing capacitor in a power supply

Diode: a p-n junction that conducts when it is forward biased and blocks current when it is reverse biased.

lessons.title: Logic Gates and Truth Tables
lessons.content:
Digital electronic circuits work with two states only. A low voltage is called logic 0, and a high voltage, such as 5 volts, is called logic 1. A logic gate is a circuit that combines these two states according to a rule, and the behaviour of a gate is written down in a truth table, a table that lists the output for every possible combination of inputs.

The three basic gates are the AND gate, the OR gate and the NOT gate. An AND gate gives 1 only when both inputs are 1, which is why it is used to test whether two conditions are met at the same time. An OR gate gives 1 when at least one input is 1. A NOT gate, also called an inverter, has a single input, and its output is the opposite of its single input, so a 1 becomes a 0 and a 0 becomes a 1.

Gates are combined to build the circuits that make decisions. A NAND gate is an AND gate followed by a NOT gate, and a NOR gate is an OR gate followed by a NOT gate; a truth table for the combination is built by working out the output of each gate in turn. Because the same few gates can be repeated millions of times on one silicon chip, they decide when a washing machine starts, when a traffic light changes, and how a calculator adds two numbers.

Write and interpret truth tables for AND, OR and NOT gates
Describe how gates are combined to make a decision circuit

Truth table: a table showing the output of a gate for every possible combination of its inputs.
AND gives 1 only when both inputs are 1, OR gives 1 when at least one input is 1, and NOT inverts its single input.

lessons.title: Impact of Electronics on Society
lessons.content:
Electronics reached the home in the 1950s through the thermionic valve, a glass device that was hot, bulky and short-lived. The transistor replaced the valve, and the integrated circuit then placed thousands, and later millions, of transistors on a single silicon chip. That one change put small and cheap computing power in phones, laptops and household appliances, so the electronics industry now brings a clear benefit to society that reaches almost every Caribbean household.

On the medical side, electronic instruments monitor a patient's heart and breathing, and imaging equipment shows doctors what is happening inside the body. In industry, automatic control keeps a factory machine working safely, checks the size of every product on a line and stops the line if something is out of place. Communication changed too: a message that once took days now travels in seconds, and distance learning reaches students far from a campus.

Each benefit carries a problem to manage. Toxic metals in discarded circuit boards must be collected and recycled, because dumping them contaminates soil and water. The energy used by data centres and by charging devices has become a large part of electricity demand, so efficient designs matter. Jobs changed or lost when a task is automated, and personal data collected by the same devices must be protected, so electronics must be used with care as well as enthusiasm.

Give examples of the benefits of electronics in medicine, industry and communication

lessons.title: Force on Current-Carrying Conductors
lessons.content:
A current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field experiences a force, and this is called the motor effect. The force is largest when the conductor is at right angles to the field, and no force is produced when the conductor lies along the field. Increasing the current, the field strength or the length of conductor in the field increases the force on the conductor, which is written as F = B I L for a conductor at right angles to the field.

The direction of the force is found with Fleming's left-hand rule: point the first finger along the field, the second finger along the current and the thumb in the direction of the force, holding the three fingers of the left hand at right angles to one another. Reversing the current or reversing the magnetic field reverses the direction of the force, and reversing both leaves the force in its original direction.

The two sides of a coil carry the current in opposite directions, so the forces on them turn the coil about its axis. That turning effect is the working principle of every electric motor and of moving-coil instruments such as the ammeter and the voltmeter.

Use Fleming's left-hand rule to predict the direction of the force
Explain how two opposite forces on a coil produce a turning effect

Fleming's left-hand rule gives the direction of the force from the field and the current.

lessons.title: DC Motor Action
lessons.content:
A simple direct current motor is a rectangular coil of insulated wire mounted between the poles of a magnet, with the ends of the coil joined to a split-ring commutator. Carbon brushes press on the commutator and connect the coil to the supply, so current flows through the coil while it rotates.

Each side of the coil carries the current in the opposite direction to the other side, so the force on one side points one way and the force on the other side points the opposite way. The two equal and opposite forces form a couple that turns the coil. Without any other part the coil would stop after half a turn, because the forces would then push it back the way it came.

The split-ring commutator solves that problem: it reverses the current in the coil every half turn, so the force on each side keeps pointing in the turning direction and the coil continues to rotate. Increasing the current, using a stronger magnet or winding more turns on the coil increases the turning effect, which is why a motor can be made to suit the job it drives.

Explain the forces on a coil in a magnetic field and the couple they produce
Explain the action of the split-ring commutator

Split-ring commutator: it reverses the current in the coil every half turn so the coil keeps turning.
The turning effect increases with the current, the strength of the magnetic field and the number of turns on the coil.

lessons.title: Radioactivity and Half-Life
lessons.content:
Radioactivity is the spontaneous and random emission of radiation from the unstable nucleus of an atom. There are three primary types of radiation: Alpha (α) particles, which are helium nuclei; Beta (β) particles, which are high-speed electrons; and Gamma (γ) rays, which are high-energy electromagnetic waves. Each type has different penetrating power and ionising ability.

Because radioactive decay is random, we cannot predict when a specific nucleus will decay. However, for a large group of atoms, the rate of decay is predictable. The half-life is the time it takes for half of the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay. For example, if a substance has a half-life of 10 years, a 100g sample will be reduced to 50g after 10 years, and then to 25g after another 10 years. A decay graph plots the count rate, the activity or the mass remaining against time, and its curve never reaches zero: the half-life is the time for the value to halve, and it is the same at every halving.

CSEC questions often involve identifying types of radiation from their properties, completing nuclear equations, and using decay curves to determine half-life. Understanding radioactivity is essential for medicine (cancer treatment), archaeology (carbon dating), and energy production (nuclear power).

Ranges and Tracks of Emissions. The range of a radiation is the distance it travels through air before it is absorbed. An alpha particle has the shortest range of the three - only a few centimetres of air - because its strong ionising power makes it lose energy very quickly. A beta particle travels much further, typically a few metres of air, because it ionises the air less densely along its path. Gamma radiation has no definite range at all: it is electromagnetic radiation, so it is not stopped at one particular distance, but is only gradually attenuated, its intensity falling as it passes through material.

A cloud chamber makes these differences visible. As a particle ionises the air it passes through, it leaves a trail of condensation droplets, and that trail shows both the range of the particle and the shape of its path:

- An alpha particle leaves a short, thick, straight track that stops abruptly, which matches its short range in air.
- A beta particle leaves a long, thin, wiggly track, because a light, fast electron is easily deflected by the air it passes through.
- A gamma ray leaves a faint, long, straight track, and it often knocks out electrons that then leave tracks of their own.

The length of a track shows how far the radiation travelled, and the thickness and straightness of the track show how densely it ionised the air - which is why cloud-chamber photographs are read as evidence about the three types of emission.

Describe the range of alpha, beta and gamma radiation in air, and the tracks each one leaves in a cloud chamber
concepts: Random Nature of Radioactive Decay: the decay of a nucleus is random, so we cannot predict which nucleus will decay next, only the rate for a large group.
Half-life is the time taken for half the nuclei to decay, and it is the same at every halving.
Half-Life and Decay Graphs: a decay graph plots the count rate, the activity or the mass remaining against time, and the half-life is read off as the time for the value to halve.

Ranges and Tracks of Emissions: an alpha particle travels only a few centimetres of air, a beta particle a few metres, and gamma radiation has no definite range because it is gradually attenuated rather than stopped at a set distance.

Cloud chamber tracks: alpha particles leave short, thick, straight tracks, beta particles leave long, thin, wiggly tracks, and gamma rays leave faint, long tracks, often with secondary electron tracks.

lessons.title: Work in Establishing the Modern Atom
lessons.content:
For more than two thousand years people have asked what matter is made of, and the answer changed whenever an experiment contradicted the model of the day. The Greek philosopher Democritus proposed tiny indivisible particles he called atoms, but the idea remained a philosophy, because no measurement could test it.

John Dalton's atomic theory, published in 1808, put atoms on a scientific footing: each element is made of identical, indestructible atoms, compounds are combinations of atoms in fixed whole-number ratios, and a chemical reaction only rearranges the atoms. Dalton's model explained the laws of chemical combination, but it treated every atom as a solid sphere with no internal structure.

At the end of the nineteenth century J. J. Thomson's experiments with cathode rays found a much lighter, negatively charged particle inside the atom, the electron. Because an atom as a whole is neutral, Thomson proposed the plum-pudding model: electrons embedded in a ball of positive charge, like fruit in a pudding.

Ernest Rutherford's alpha-particle scattering experiment in 1911 overturned that model. A small number of alpha particles were deflected through large angles and some came straight back, which is possible only if the positive charge is concentrated in a tiny, dense centre: the nucleus. Niels Bohr's model extended the picture in 1913 by placing electrons in fixed shells, which explained the sharp spectral lines that the plum-pudding model could not explain.

The pattern of the whole story is that a model survives only while it explains the evidence. Each new experiment kept the parts that still worked and replaced the one part that did not.

Explain the evidence that replaced each model

Thomson's plum-pudding model: electrons embedded in a ball of positive charge.
Rutherford's nucleus: the positive charge is concentrated in a tiny, dense centre, as alpha-particle scattering showed.

lessons.title: Geiger-Marsden Experiment and Nuclear Structure
lessons.content:
In 1909 Ernest Rutherford, working with Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden, fired alpha particles at a very thin gold foil in a vacuum and counted where they went with a zinc sulphide screen that flashed when a particle struck it. Most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil, and the flashes confirmed that they had crossed it with almost no change of direction.

A small number of alpha particles were deflected through large angles, and a few alpha particles came straight back towards the source, about one in every 8000. A deflected alpha particle behaves in that way only if it has met a concentrated positive charge: an alpha particle is positive, so a positive nucleus repels it.

From these observations Rutherford concluded that most of the atom is empty space, that all the positive charge and nearly all the mass sit in a tiny nucleus, and that the electrons occupy the rest of the atom. The nucleus is about 10 to the power minus 15 metres across, roughly a hundred thousand times smaller than the atom itself, which is about 10 to the power minus 10 metres.

The experiment also gave the charge on the nucleus a meaning. The number of units of positive charge equals the atomic number, which is the position of the element in the periodic table, and the electrons that balance that charge must therefore equal it in number.

lessons.title: Atomic Composition and Neutrality
lessons.content:
Every atom is built from three subatomic particles. A proton carries a positive charge and sits in the nucleus. A neutron has no charge and about the same mass as a proton, and it also sits in the nucleus. An electron carries a negative charge, has almost no mass compared with a proton, and occupies the shells around the nucleus.

The number of protons decides which element an atom is: this is the atomic number, Z. The mass number, A, is the number of protons plus the number of neutrons, so counted with the protons, the neutrons give the mass number. A nucleus of carbon-12 therefore holds six protons and six neutrons.

An atom as a whole is neutral, because the number of protons equals the number of electrons. Charge is not created or destroyed when an ion forms: an atom gains or loses electrons and the proton count does not change. Losing an electron leaves one more proton than electron, so the particle becomes a positive ion, and gaining an electron gives a negative ion.

Inside the nucleus the protons and neutrons are held together by the strong nuclear force, which acts over the tiny distances between them and is far stronger than the electric repulsion of the protons. The electrons are held to the atom by the electric attraction between their negative charge and the positive nucleus.

lessons.title: Nuclide Notation and Isotopes
lessons.content:
A nuclide is a particular nucleus, and it is written with the mass number as a superscript before the symbol and the atomic number as a subscript. Carbon-12 has 6 protons and 6 neutrons, and it is written with 12 above and 6 below the symbol C, while carbon-14 has 6 protons and 8 neutrons.

Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. Isotopes of an element behave identically in chemical reactions, because the chemistry is decided by the electrons and isotopes have the same number of electrons. They differ in mass number, in density, and in the rate at which they take part in physical processes such as diffusion.

Hydrogen has three isotopes: protium with one proton and no neutrons, deuterium with one proton and one neutron, and tritium with one proton and two neutrons. The relative atomic mass of an element is the weighted average of the masses of its isotopes, which is why the relative atomic mass of chlorine is about 35.5 although no single chlorine atom has that mass.

Some isotopes are radioactive and others are stable. Carbon-14 is radioactive and is used for dating, while carbon-12 is stable and makes up almost all the carbon on Earth. How many electrons an ion has is found from the atomic number, not from the mass number.

lessons.title: Shell Model and the Periodic Table
lessons.content:
In the shell model the electrons of an atom are arranged in shells around the nucleus. The first shell holds up to 2 electrons and the second and third hold up to 8, and the shells fill from the inside outwards. Sodium has eleven electrons and the configuration 2, 8, 1.

An element's place in the periodic table follows from its shells. The group number equals the number of electrons in the outer shell, so every element of group 1 has one outer electron and every element of group 7 has seven. The period number equals the number of occupied shells, so the elements of period 3 have electrons in three shells.

The outer electrons decide how an element behaves chemically. Sodium with one outer electron loses it to form a positive ion, and chlorine with seven outer electrons gains one to form a negative ion, so both end up with a full outer shell. Electrons in a full outer shell are held firmly and are not easily removed.

The noble gases of group 8 have a full outer shell, so they are unreactive: helium has 2 outer electrons and the rest of the group have 8. The shell model therefore explains the shape of the periodic table rather than merely describing it. It also shows its own limit, because it says nothing about the nucleus and cannot explain radioactivity.

The group number equals the number of electrons in the outer shell.
The period number equals the number of occupied shells.

lessons.title: Marie Curie's Work and Radioactivity
lessons.content:
In 1896 Henri Becquerel found that uranium salts fogged a photographic plate even when they had not been exposed to sunlight. Marie Curie took up the puzzle, and with her husband Pierre Curie showed that the rays came from the uranium atoms themselves rather than from a chemical reaction, and she gave the process the name radioactivity.

The Curies processed tonnes of pitchblende, a uranium ore, and in 1898 they separated two new elements that were far more radioactive than uranium: polonium and radium. Radium was about a million times more radioactive than uranium, and isolating it took years of chemical work, with tonnes of ore yielding a fraction of a gram.

Becquerel and the Curies shared the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1903, and Marie Curie was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1911 for the discovery of radium and polonium and for her study of the nature of these new elements. She was the first person to win a Nobel Prize twice.

The discovery changed both physics and medicine. Radium was used in early cancer treatment, and radioactive isotopes later became medical tracers. The work also showed the hazards: the Curies and their assistants handled radioactive material without shielding and their health suffered, which is why the safety precautions used today exist.

lessons.title: Effects of Electric and Magnetic Fields on Emissions
lessons.content:
An electric field exerts a force on any charged particle and none on a neutral one, so the three emissions behave differently between two charged plates. A beam of alpha particles bends towards the negative plate, because an alpha particle is positive. A beam of beta particles bends towards the positive plate, and so in the opposite direction to the alpha beam.

The amount of bending depends on the charge and the mass of the particle. A beta particle is deflected far more than an alpha particle: it is negative and it is much lighter, and a light particle is deflected more by the same force. Gamma rays pass through undeflected, because they carry no charge.

A magnetic field bends charged particles too, and the force acts at right angles to both the field and the direction of travel. Alpha particles bend one way and beta particles bend the opposite way, because their charges are opposite, and the beta deflection is again much the greater. Gamma rays are not deflected by a magnetic field at all.

Deflections like these are how the three emissions were told apart in the laboratory, and the same principle is used today to focus a beam of charged particles or to separate ions of different mass.

lessons.title: Interpreting Nuclear Reactions
lessons.content:
A nuclear reaction is written as an equation with the mass number and the atomic number of each nuclide, and the equation must balance on both counts. In the alpha decay of uranium-238 the equation is uranium-238 giving thorium-234 plus an alpha particle: the mass numbers balance because 238 equals 234 plus 4, and the atomic numbers balance because 92 equals 90 plus 2.

In beta decay the mass number is unchanged and the atomic number rises by one. Carbon-14 decays to nitrogen-14 plus a beta particle: 14 balances with 14 plus 0, and 6 balances with 7 plus minus 1. The beta particle is written with a mass number of 0 and an atomic number of minus 1, because it is an electron.

Gamma emission is written with no change to either number, which is why a gamma ray is often left out of a decay equation. In every case the particle missing from a partly written equation is found by making the mass numbers and the atomic numbers add up on each side.

The same rule covers artificial transmutation. In 1919 Rutherford passed alpha particles through nitrogen gas and found that nitrogen-14 had changed into oxygen-17 plus a proton, and an equation of that kind identifies the product of any bombardment.

Use conservation of mass number and charge to find a missing particle

In beta decay the mass number is unchanged and the atomic number rises by 1.

lessons.title: Applications of Radio-Isotopes
lessons.content:
A radio-isotope is chosen for a job by its half-life and by the radiation it emits. For use inside the body the half-life should be short, so that the dose does not last, and the emission should be gamma rays, which leave the body instead of being absorbed by it. Technetium-99m is used as a tracer in medical imaging, where a gamma camera follows it through an organ, and this is the commonest use in medicine.

Cobalt-60 emits gamma rays and is used in radiotherapy to destroy cancer cells, and it is also used to sterilise medical equipment and food. A strongly ionising alpha emitter is used where its short range is an advantage: americium-241 is the alpha source in a smoke detector, where its alpha particles ionise the air and allow a small current to flow.

In industry a beta or gamma source measures the thickness of paper, plastic or metal as the material passes between the source and a detector, and a tracer added to a pipeline shows up a leak. In agriculture phosphorus-32 follows the uptake of fertiliser by a plant, and radiation is used to breed new varieties of crop.

In archaeology carbon-14 is used for dating once-living material, because a living thing takes in carbon until it dies and its carbon-14 then decays with a half-life of about 5700 years, so the activity left shows how long ago it died. Uranium-238, with a half-life of about 4500 million years, dates rocks.

Explain how the half-life and the type of emission decide which isotope is chosen

Cobalt-60 is used in radiotherapy and to sterilise medical equipment and food.

lessons.title: Energy from Nuclear Reactions
lessons.content:
A nuclear reaction releases energy because the total mass of the products is slightly less than the total mass of the reactants. The difference is called the mass defect, and the small loss of mass appears as energy according to the equation E = mc squared, where c is the speed of light. Because the speed of light is large, a tiny mass corresponds to a very large amount of energy.

Nuclear fission is the splitting of a heavy nucleus. A uranium-235 nucleus that absorbs a neutron becomes unstable and splits into two lighter nuclei, releasing two or three neutrons and a large amount of energy. The neutrons released by fission can cause further fissions, so the process can become a chain reaction: in a reactor the chain reaction is controlled, and in a weapon it is not.

Nuclear fusion is the joining of light nuclei. In the Sun hydrogen nuclei join to form helium, releasing energy and needing extremely high temperatures and pressures to bring the nuclei close enough to fuse. Fusion releases more energy per kilogram of fuel than fission and produces less long-lived radioactive waste, but it has not yet been made to work as a power source on Earth.

For the same mass of fuel a nuclear reaction releases far more energy than burning coal, oil or gas, which is why a nuclear power station needs only a small mass of uranium each year.

lessons.title: Utilisation of Nuclear Energy
lessons.content:
A nuclear power station uses the heat from a controlled fission chain reaction to make steam, which drives turbines that turn generators. The fuel is uranium, usually enriched in uranium-235 and sealed inside fuel rods. A moderator such as graphite or water slows the fast neutrons down so that they can cause further fission, control rods of boron or cadmium absorb neutrons, and a coolant carries the heat away to the boiler.

Each part of the reactor has one job, and the design is meant to keep the reaction from running away. The control rods are pushed in to absorb more neutrons and reduce the power and pulled out to raise it; thick concrete and steel shielding stops neutrons and gamma rays reaching the people outside; and the used fuel is stored under water, which removes its heat and shields the radiation.

The advantages of nuclear power are large: a small mass of fuel gives a very large amount of energy, and generating electricity this way does not produce carbon dioxide or the other gases that cause acid rain. The disadvantages are large too. The used fuel is radioactive waste that stays hazardous for thousands of years, so it must be stored and shielded; a reactor is expensive to build and to decommission; uranium is a non-renewable fuel; and an accident releases radioactive material into the surroundings.

The decision is a judgement about which risks a country will accept. Jamaica generates its electricity mainly from oil and gas and has no nuclear power station, so nuclear power is an option for countries with the grid, the money and the regulatory system to run it safely. Radiation safety itself rests on three ideas: shielding, distance and time.
